1.goal: To open the lesson that closes the block, and to say in one sentence what it is.
1.interaction: T speaks; S listens. One minute.
run: THIS LESSON CLOSES THE BLOCK. Read the records of the three previous lessons before you start — they are what the planning of the next block comes out of.
Say in one sentence what today is: the whole check-in, from good morning to thank you.
Do not preview the surprise question.
exact: What today is: "Today you do the whole check-in. From good morning to thank you."
1.expected: She knows the shape of the hour before it starts.
1.support: If she looks worried, name what she already has: three lessons of sentences, and all of them are used today.
1.challenge: Ask her to guess how many things she will have to say.
1.monitoring: Whether closing the block registers with her as an ending or as a test.
1.evidence: Nothing yet. This screen is the frame for the four that follow.
1.transition: Move on when she is on the next screen.

2.goal: To place the scene of the whole lesson: she arrives, the desk asks, she answers, and at some point she asks for something.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Read the scene with her.
Confirm: she arrives, the desk asks, she answers — and at some point she asks for one thing.
DO NOT PREVIEW THE TAXI QUESTION.
2.expected: She can say what she is about to do, in one sentence.
2.support: If she is unsure what "asking for one thing" means, name one example she already has: a room with a window.
2.challenge: Ask what she would want to ask for at a real hotel.
2.monitoring: Whether she treats the request as part of the check-in or as an extra.
2.evidence: What she says she would ask for. It becomes the content of stage 6.
2.transition: Move on when she knows what she is about to do.

3.goal: The whole check-in with NO model. This attempt is half of today's evidence.
3.interaction: Role-play. You are Emma at the desk.
run: Nothing on screen. Open the desk and wait.
DO NOT CORRECT AND DO NOT SUGGEST. If she freezes for more than ten seconds, give the FIRST WORD of the sentence and only that.
Write down four things: did she greet? did she say her name? did she confirm the dates? did she ask for anything?
exact: Opening, as Emma: "Good afternoon! Checking in?"
If she freezes for more than ten seconds, the first word and only that: "My…" / "I have…" / "Two…"
3.expected: An incomplete check-in. The greeting and the request are the two that usually go missing, and that is what stages 4 and 5 exist for.
3.support: The first word of the sentence, and nothing more. Do not finish it and do not rephrase it.
3.challenge: Say nothing after her first sentence and let the silence ask the next question.
3.monitoring: The four items above, and how long each silence lasts.
3.evidence: The unmodeled attempt: which of the four moments she produced on her own. Half of today's evidence, and taken before any input.
3.transition: Move on when she has finished — even with half of it missing.

4.goal: To show the four moments of a check-in, AFTER her own attempt.
4.interaction: S classifies on screen, T checks.
run: She classifies the six lines. Discuss only what she got wrong.
CCQ: what costs two words and changes the whole tone? (Good morning and thank you.)
If she skipped the greeting at stage 3 — and almost everybody does — this is where it comes up, without embarrassment.
4.expected: Six placed. The two at the end are the ones that get argued about.
4.support: If a line is hard to place, ask when she would say it: on the way in, or on the way out.
4.challenge: Ask her to add one line of her own to each of the three moments.
4.monitoring: Whether she notices on her own that she skipped the greeting.
4.evidence: Whether the missing move is visible to her once the shape is on screen.
4.transition: Move on when the six are in place.

5.goal: For her to see that she already has the three moves for an unexpected question.
5.interaction: S marks on screen, then T–S discussion.
run: She marks the three that work.
Then ask where those sentences came from. (Lesson 2.)
Let her be the one to say that she already has what she needs.
5.expected: In her own words: this is not new content — she has had it since lesson 2.
5.support: If she does not make the connection, name lesson 2 and let her find the two sentences herself.
5.challenge: Ask which of the three she would use for a question she did not understand at all.
5.monitoring: Whether she recognizes her own repertoire, or treats every screen as new material.
5.evidence: Whether she can name where a sentence came from. It is the difference between collecting phrases and having a repertoire.
5.transition: Move on when she has recognized the three.

6.goal: To make one opening automatic — Can I have…? — and to keep the two repair sentences warm.
6.interaction: T prompts, S produces. Fast, one at a time.
run: The five requests with Can I have…?, one at a time, quickly.
Then the two repair sentences.
Correct immediately and gently. After this stage there is no more correcting until the feedback.
CLOSE EVERYTHING ON SCREEN before round 1.
exact: The prompts, one at a time: "A room with a window." / "The wifi password." / "Breakfast at seven." / "A taxi on Saturday." / "A late check-out."
The correction, in one word, then straight on: "Can I have."
6.expected: Five requests with the same opening, and the two repair sentences without hesitation.
6.support: Give the opening — Can I… — and let her finish.
6.challenge: Ask for a sixth request that is not on the list.
6.monitoring: Whether the opening comes without a decision, or is rebuilt each time.
6.evidence: Whether Can I have…? has become one block or is still three words.
6.transition: Move on when the five requests have come out.

7.goal: The whole check-in, with one question nobody showed her.
7.interaction: Role-play. You play both parts: Emma at the desk and, at the end, Rui with the taxi question.
run: The whole check-in. When she is nearly closing, play the recorded question ONCE.
If she asks for a repeat, play it again and COUNT IT AS A SUCCESS — it is the move from lesson 2, and it is what this cycle measures.
If she answers only yes or no, that is correct. It is a yes-or-no question.
Do not correct during. Write down what she says, as she says it.
exact: Opening, as Emma: "Good afternoon! Welcome to Hotel Marina."
When she asks for a repeat: "Of course." — and play it again, with nothing added.
If she stops after the question, hand the turn back: "So — Saturday. Is that a yes?"
7.expected: The four moments, and a yes or a no to the taxi question — with or without a repeat first.
7.support: Play it again. That is the whole support, and asking for it is the point.
7.challenge: Add a second unexpected question, this one about breakfast times.
7.monitoring: Whether she asks for the repeat, and whether the check-in survives the interruption.
7.evidence: How she handled the question nobody had shown her. This is the criterion the whole block was built for.
7.transition: Move on when she has answered the taxi question.

8.goal: To give back two things, and to ask the question the previous course made necessary.
run: Two things, and one of them positive and concrete.
ASK ABOUT THE PRE-CLASSES — whether she opened all four, and what she thought of them. It was the most critical point of her previous experience. Write the answer down in her own words.
Do not add content. Round 2 is the same check-in, shorter.
exact: The question about the pre-class, asked plainly: "Did you open the four pre-classes? What did you think of them?"
8.expected: An honest answer about the pre-class, whatever it is. A negative answer is more useful than a polite one.
8.support: If the answer is polite and empty, ask which of the four she actually finished.
8.challenge: Ask which activity she would drop, and why.
8.monitoring: Whether the pre-class is being used, and whether it asked for anything she had no way of knowing.
8.evidence: Her answer about the pre-class, in her own words. The planning of the next block starts here.
8.transition: Move on when the two points and the pre-class question are done.

9.goal: The same check-in in thirty seconds, to see what she cuts.
9.interaction: Role-play, timed. There is a queue behind her.
run: The same check-in in thirty seconds, with a queue behind her.
Watch what she cuts. If the greeting and the thank you go, only information is left — and those two are what change how the desk answers.
Write down what survived.
exact: Setting it up: "There are four people behind you. Thirty seconds. Go."
9.expected: Name, dates and one request survive. The greeting and the thank you are the ones at risk.
9.support: If she freezes under the clock, drop the clock and keep the queue. The pressure is the point, not the number.
9.challenge: Run it once more in twenty seconds.
9.monitoring: What she cuts first. It tells you what is automatic and what is still being assembled.
9.evidence: What survived at speed. Compare it with the unmodeled attempt at stage 3 — same task, two conditions, one lesson apart.
9.transition: Move on when the thirty seconds are done.

10.goal: To close the block out loud, with what exists now that did not exist two weeks ago.
10.interaction: T–S. She ticks what she recognizes.
run: She marks what she recognizes on screen.

CLOSE THE BLOCK WITH HER, OUT LOUD: four lessons, and a whole check-in in English with a question she was not expecting. Two weeks ago she had not said one sentence — and she had left a course concluding that the problem was her.
Say the homework out loud, and do not put it on screen: the post-class has the whole check-in to record on her own, and two free resources.

Fill in the block record before you close: did she produce a whole sentence with no model in all four lessons? did she do the pre-classes, and what did she say about them? The planning of the next lessons starts from those two answers.
exact: Closing the block: "Two weeks ago you had not said one sentence in English. Today you did a whole check-in, and you handled a question nobody had shown you."
10.expected: Some of the items ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If she ticks nothing, read the list with her and ask which one she could do at a real desk.
10.challenge: Ask which of the four lessons she would repeat, and why.
10.monitoring: Where she puts herself now, against where she put herself in lesson 1.
10.evidence: The block record: whole sentence with no model across the four lessons, and her answer about the pre-class. Both decide the next block.
